title: AI-prefilled organizers and automatic chasing of missing client documents
problem: Collecting client information and documents means repeated emails and late files, and one missing brokerage statement can hold up a whole return.
approach: Canopy offers AI-prefilled questionnaires that clients confirm or change, plus AI file classification; Basis and ApariPro describe agents that chase clients.
Canopy says firms can save as much as 20 minutes per client (vendor-published).
Staff review request lists and open items; the preparer still conducts the due-diligence interview and signs Form 8867.

title: Reading tax documents and K-1 footnotes with confidence flags and exception review
problem: K-1 packages and multi-tier partnerships defeat template scanning and manual keying, and an extraction error can flow into a return without any flag.
approach: CCH Axcess Scan (Wolters Kluwer) extracts figures and surfaces only exceptions; Wolters Kluwer says K-1 extraction averages 97.5% accuracy (vendor-published).
PwC agents rate each K-1 footnote item with a confidence level and flag it; one reviewer now replaces three people (self-reported).
Reviewers override low-confidence mappings with a recorded reason and compare extracted figures to source documents.

title: Retail tax offices use AI to cut data entry for advice
problem: Preparers in assisted-tax offices spend much of an appointment collecting and entering information, leaving less time for advice.
approach: H&R Block management said it is automating mechanical tax preparation work, from manual data entry to the initial review of prior-year returns.
The advice-focused model runs in pilot offices; H&R Block reported higher client satisfaction, with no figures given (self-reported).
Tax pros remain responsible for the returns and the client guidance.

title: Agent drafts a simple personal tax return for CPA review
problem: Preparing even simple personal returns means sorting documents, keying data and building the return by hand, which crowds out higher-value work in a short season.
approach: Thomson Reuters' Ready to Review uses agents to extract data from documents and prior returns and draft returns linked to sources.
An early-adopter partner at CLH CPAs and Consultants said it saves about an hour per simple return (vendor-published).
Professionals review the draft, diagnostics and source links before delivery; the taxpayer reviews before signing the e-file authorisation.
who: Thomson Reuters, CLH CPAs and Consultants

title: Agent prepares complex personal returns end to end for CPA sign-off
problem: Complex returns with many K-1s, brokerage statements and multiple states take days of preparer and reviewer time, and firms are short of staff in busy season.
approach: Black Ore, Basis, Accrual and OpenAI describe agents that extract data, apply tax logic, build workpapers and feed the firm's tax software.
OpenAI says Tax AI processed 7,000 returns in a Crete pilot and saves about a third of preparation time (vendor-published).
Boulay's partner says returns with 60-70+ K-1s fell from over 100 hours to about 15-20 hours (vendor-published).
A CPA reviews and signs off, ties workpapers to source documents and answers questions the system cannot resolve.
who: Black Ore, Basis, Accrual, OpenAI, Crete

title: Agent prepares partnership, S corporation and trust returns through to K-1s
problem: Partnership and trust returns need trial-balance import, allocations, depreciation and basis tracking, and K-1 tie-out, much of it built in spreadsheets, so review burden multiplies.
approach: Accrual describes preparing partnership and trust returns through to K-1s, with Armanino named as customer; Basis demonstrated an agent completing a 1065.
Armanino statistics on Accrual's page show an estimated 50% reduction in federal preparation and review effort (vendor-published).
Practitioners review drafts and open items, approve agent changes and sign the return.

title: Trial balance to tax workpapers for pass-through business returns
problem: Business returns start with mapping the client's trial balance to return lines and building book-to-tax and fixed-asset workpapers by hand.
approach: Basis agents map client accounts to return lines, flag unmapped accounts and draft book-to-tax and fixed-asset workpapers with figures cited to source.
A Whitcomb & Sheridan partner says a 2-3 hour task takes about 30 minutes (vendor-published); the quote does not name this step.
Staff review mapping exceptions and workpaper drafts.

title: Agent works inside the firm's own tax software and documents each entry
problem: Pre-preparation tools push data into the tax engine, so the firm still does the final steps by hand.
approach: TaxGPT's agent signs in to the firm's tax software, enters data, works through diagnostics and documents every entry back to its source.
TaxGPT claims a 50% cut in first-pass preparation time on its product page (vendor-published).
The firm's team reviews and signs off, and the firm's software stays the system of record.

title: General-purpose agents run practitioner-taught routines and build return workpapers
problem: Multi-source follow-up on a return, such as call notes, open issues, binders and signature requests, is done by hand across systems.
approach: Accrual's Arc, unveiled September 2026, drafts a plan, asks approval, then updates workpapers with an audit trail; no outcome figures are published.
A practitioner, Sam Leon, uses Claude Cowork to prepare returns; the episode title claims 5x faster (self-reported).
The practitioner approves the plan and each proposed change.

title: Use a deterministic engine to calculate returns; language model for intake
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: unaided language models calculate returns unreliably, so calculation errors, wrong tax tables and eligibility mistakes are costly and hard to audit.
approach: Researchers recommend pairing the model with a deterministic calculation engine or symbolic solver, with the model handling intake, explanation and orchestration.
In a benchmark of 51 simplified returns, the best of four models computed 32.35% correctly under the strict test (vendor-published).
The preparer reviews the engine-calculated return and any model-supplied inputs.

title: Grounded assistant for tax preparers, with every cited authority checked
problem: Tax pros must keep up with code changes and answer unusual client questions, and general models can invent authorities, as a 2026 Tax Court case about hallucinated citations showed.
approach: H&R Block and OpenAI said in April 2025 they were building an assistant grounded in Tax Institute data; management later reported adoption.
No usage counts or accuracy figures were published (self-reported).
The tax pro decides how to answer the client; a reviewer opens and reads each cited authority.

title: AI-assisted return review with source tie-out, diagnostics and prior-year comparison
problem: Reviewers must check figures against source documents and prior years, which takes senior time, and review becomes the bottleneck when preparation gets faster.
approach: Intuit ProConnect runs an AI assistant against thousands of diagnostics; Basis, Accrual and Thomson Reuters tie figures to source and flag exceptions.
TaxGPT launched a return-review agent that surfaces audit-sensitive items; PwC lists tax diagnostics among its deployed agents.
No error counts are published; one user says the checks give it confidence (vendor-published).
The reviewer inspects flagged exceptions and decides treatments; the preparer or reviewer signs.
who: Intuit, Basis, Accrual, Thomson Reuters, TaxGPT, PwC

title: Review controls for AI-assisted returns: decision logs, override monitoring, escalation
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: as AI raises volume, partners may spend less time per return, and a firm with no record cannot show what the tool suggested.
approach: Log every AI suggestion and the preparer's decision (accept, modify, reject) with rationale, and review override rates by preparer monthly.
Scale sampling and spot checks to volume, and escalate novel or uncertain positions to senior review regardless of the AI's confidence.
Sign-off must evidence real analysis; regulators such as Australia's TPB and the IRS OPR expect AI steps to be verified and documented.

title: Automated look-back review of prior-year returns offered to every new client
problem: Second Look, a review of a new client's last three years of returns for missed opportunities, was manual, so tax pros rarely offered it to new clients.
approach: H&R Block management said it automated Second Look over about 18 months with newer AI, so many more new clients opt in.
Management said Second Look clients returned at a rate over 600 basis points higher; uncontrolled, not due to automation alone (self-reported).
Tax pros focus on the returns with the greatest opportunity.

title: AI-drafted client messages and return explanations, reviewed before sending
problem: Clients call to ask where their return stands, preparers write explanatory letters by hand, and firms cannot paste client data into public AI tools.
approach: Short status messages are generated when a job changes stage, and practitioners use AI to draft correspondence.
WCG plans a SOC 2-compliant, zero-data-retention sandbox for client narratives, quotes and tax-plan comparisons from returns; Intuit lists an AI Client Briefing.
The preparer reads and edits every client communication before it is sent; no outcome figures are published.

title: Automating return assembly, delivery and e-signature authorisation
problem: Assembling the return package, collecting signatures, including the Form 8879 e-file authorisation, and taking payment are manual and error-prone.
approach: SafeSend and SurePrep from Thomson Reuters are mostly workflow automation; the vendor claims an AI layer that recognises documents and flags discrepancies.
Thomson Reuters says firms using SafeSend save about 15 minutes per return (vendor-published).
The preparer signs the return and the taxpayer reviews it before signing Form 8879.

title: UK self assessment and Making Tax Digital preparation with AI document processing
problem: UK firms chase clients for information, review documents manually and re-key data into tax software for self assessment returns and quarterly Making Tax Digital submissions.
approach: ApariPro says it automates client information collection, AI processing of documents such as P60s, return population and submission, integrating with CCH iFirm.
No figures are published; anonymous testimonials say manual data entry fell (vendor-published).
The team reviews and approves all information before submission.

title: Phased adoption: simple returns first, scope gates, parallel runs on prior-year returns
problem: Firms adopt AI preparation on vendor claims and cannot say whether time, quality or cycle time improved, and vendors bundle extraction, deduction suggestion and position drafting together.
approach: Practitioners advise starting with simpler returns, rerunning last year's returns to compare with what was filed, and recording cycle times first.
An AICPA case study (an idea) authorises the tool in phases, with gates such as a hallucination rate of 2% or less.
A reviewer compares the AI's version with the filed return; named partners sign off each phase. No parallel-run result is published.

title: Firm AI policy, approved-tool list and vendor due diligence for tax practices
problem: Staff use AI tools whether or not the firm has sanctioned them, nobody owns AI, and firms cannot show how outputs were verified or what happens to sensitive return data.
approach: The IRS Office of Professional Responsibility says firms should have AI policies covering training, data handling and accuracy monitoring, and vet vendors.
Guidance adds an approved-tool list, an AI lead or committee, and client data restricted to enterprise-approved AI under the written security plan.
Thomson Reuters reports more than one-third of professionals use AI tools their firm has not sanctioned (vendor-published).
A principal or AI committee approves tools before client use; the managing partner and counsel sign off vendor contracts.
who: IRS OPR, Thomson Reuters, Wolters Kluwer, AICPA

title: Dedicated AI team, champion network and training that protects the junior pipeline
problem: Tools change faster than firm processes, regulators make AI competence personal to the preparer, and AI is automating the entry-level tasks juniors learn on.
approach: PwC reports a governance committee, an Agent OS controlling agent tools, more than 3,200 AI champions and a training programme (self-reported).
WCG says its AI Tax Prep Pod launches in November 2026 to design workflows, test tools and document best practice.
An AICPA framework proposes tool-independent tax-law training and an annual check that staff can handle complex matters without the tool.

title: Client disclosure and consent wording before AI touches return information
problem: Section 7216 requires written consent for some uses of return information, and it is unsettled whether an AI tool counts as software or as a third party.
approach: Practitioners and the AICPA advise a signed stand-alone AI consent, an inventory of AI tools touching client data and security-plan governance.
Consent must be knowing, voluntary, signed, dated and not retroactive; no rule requiring disclosure of AI use was found.
The client signs and dates before any use; counsel reviews the language before the tool touches any client matter.
who: IRS OPR, AICPA, Tax Practitioners Board

title: Reprice return work from hours to value or bundled fees
problem: This is an idea under dispute: hourly billing shrinks when AI cuts preparation time, and billing for time not spent may breach the bar on unconscionable fees.
approach: Price by value, bundle preparation with advisory services, and disclose and credit AI efficiencies, as the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility describes.
The AICPA disputes that language, saying it does not appear to allow value pricing and overlooks software and governance costs.
The partner approves the fee basis and the client agrees it in the engagement letter.

title: Replace offshore or contract data entry and first-pass preparation with AI
problem: Busy-season volume is met with outsourced, contract and offshore preparers, which raises onboarding, quality and disclosure concerns.
approach: Firms bring first-pass preparation onshore through AI products instead of staffing it offshore or with contractors.
A vendor founder says users talk of bringing work onshore; a consultant says AI affects outsourcing more than onshore staff. No figures.
A partner reviews the AI-prepared return.

title: AI-native roll-up buys small tax practices and runs them on in-house AI
problem: Small tax practices carry heavy manual workloads and thin margins and find it hard to adopt new processes, while buyers look for recurring-revenue service businesses.
approach: Multiplier acquired Citrine International Tax, a 12-person cross-border tax boutique, and applied AI tools it built in-house.
TechCrunch reports the tools helped Citrine more than double its profit margins (self-reported).
The source does not describe human checkpoints.

title: Taxpayers use general-purpose AI agents to draft or check their own returns
problem: Self-filers face cost, jargon and complex forms, and some now ask general-purpose AI for help before, or instead of, hiring a preparer.
approach: Perplexity announced Computer for Taxes in April 2026, which maps uploaded documents to IRS forms and drafts a federal return.
A TaxSlayer test of four chatbots found refund errors averaging more than $2,000 across eight scenarios (vendor-published).
By design there is no human checkpoint for self-filers; practitioners are asked to validate client-brought AI conclusions.
